- If sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly, especially after sharp spikes.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) or neutral (0.00), model often underestimates; adjust upward, particularly if recent prices are trending up.
- After a price spike, model frequently overshoots and fails to correct — apply a “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast by 1–2% for each subsequent day post-spike.
- When sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish, model often lags — forecast should be adjusted downward 1–3 days ahead of true reversal.
- Mean reversion is strong in 30-day horizon — if forecast is >10% above recent 18-day average, reduce by 1–2% per day until convergence.
- If sentiment history shows high volatility (alternating 0.33/1.00), model tends to smooth too much — allow for 2–3% asymmetric adjustment toward true volatility peaks.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows a sharp drop after a peak, model often fails to anticipate — add a “drop buffer” rule: reduce forecast by 2–5% if sentiment turns negative within 3 days.
